timeline.body: After the September 11 attacks, Congress passes the Aviation and Transportation Security Act, federalizing airport security under a new Transportation Security Administration.
The Homeland Security Act consolidates 22 federal agencies into the Department of Homeland Security, creating ICE and placing TSA under its umbrella.
DHS becomes the third-largest federal department, but its funding depends on annual appropriations bills that Congress routinely fails to pass on time.
Federal law classifies TSA screeners as "essential" employees, meaning they must report to work during a shutdown — but receive no paycheck until Congress restores funding.
For two decades after its founding, TSA denied its roughly 60,000 officers collective bargaining rights, leaving them with fewer labor protections than nearly any other federal workforce.
"Essential" is a designation that compels labor without compensation — a category that applies to the lowest-paid federal employees screening every passenger in the country.
The longest government shutdown in US history runs 35 days over border wall funding; TSA agents unable to pay rent or fuel call in sick en masse, causing hours-long airport security lines.
Food banks set up stations inside federal buildings to feed unpaid workers; Congress eventually passes back pay weeks after the shutdown ends.
The 2018–2019 shutdown demonstrated that the people Congress considers essential enough to compel are the same people it considers expendable enough to stop paying.
A second DHS funding lapse leaves TSA agents again screening passengers without pay while security lines grow at major airports.
ICE expands visible enforcement operations at commercial airports during the shutdown, turning terminals into sites of immigration policing.
Delta Air Lines suspends its VIP Congressional escort service at airports — a pointed withdrawal of privilege from the lawmakers responsible for the impasse.
Senate leaders signal a deal is reportedly imminent to restore DHS funding and end the standoff.

tsa-ice-dhs-shutdown.label: TSA workers unpaid in second shutdown as ICE militarizes airports

timeline.body: CIA and MI6 overthrew Prime Minister Mosaddegh after he nationalized Iranian oil, ending Iran's democratic experiment and installing Shah Pahlavi as a Western client ruler.
The Iranian Revolution toppled the Shah; the Islamic Republic severed all ties with both the United States and Israel, redefining the region's power map.
Iraq invaded Iran with Western and Gulf Arab backing, killing half a million people in the longest conventional war of the twentieth century.
The USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 civilians aboard — an event seared into Iranian collective memory and never formally apologized for.
The Strait of Hormuz is 104 miles long and as narrow as 24 miles, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the open ocean beyond.
Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply passes through it daily — whoever controls the strait holds a hand on the throat of the global economy.
The Tanker War saw Iran and Iraq attack over 450 merchant vessels in the Gulf, drawing US naval escorts and setting the precedent for militarized shipping lanes.
Iran has repeatedly threatened to close Hormuz in response to sanctions or military threats, making the strait the Islamic Republic's most potent asymmetric lever.
The JCPOA nuclear deal traded Iranian enrichment limits for sanctions relief, briefly opening a diplomatic channel between Tehran and Washington.
The Trump administration unilaterally withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed maximum-pressure sanctions, collapsing the diplomatic framework.
The US assassinated IRGC commander Qasem Soleimani at Baghdad airport, bringing Iran and America closer to open war than at any point since 1988.
The Abraham Accords normalized relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco — Iran viewed the agreements as an encirclement strategy.
Iran and Israel exchanged direct missile and drone strikes for the first time, ending decades of shadow war through proxies.
The six GCC monarchies — Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman — sit on the southern shore of the Gulf, caught between US security guarantees and Iranian missiles minutes away.
Bahrain and the UAE signed the Abraham Accords; Saudi Arabia has been courted but has not, conditioning normalization on Palestinian statehood.
Any Gulf military entry risks turning economic infrastructure — desalination plants, oil terminals, shipping lanes — into targets for Iranian retaliation.
Trump claims Iran gave an unspecified 'prize' on Hormuz as the blockade tightens and diplomatic signals grow increasingly contradictory.
Pakistani and Afghan clerics call to extend the military pause through Eid al-Adha, invoking the Islamic tradition of sacred truces during holy periods.
Gulf states weigh direct military involvement for the first time, a decision that would shatter decades of hedging between Washington and Tehran.
"And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also] and rely upon Allah. Indeed, it is He who is the Hearing, the Knowing." — Quran 8:61
Ibn Kathir: This verse commands acceptance of genuine peace overtures, citing the Prophet's acceptance of the Treaty of Hudaybiyah even when companions doubted its terms.
